klo: Define strategy architecture and articulate strategic intent in relation to the organisation’s purpose, long-term value and stakeholder relevance.
Define a coherent future position and the organisational meaning of success.
Evaluate the consistency between strategic ambition, organisational identity and the realities of the operating environment.
Establish a shared strategic direction that supports consistent enterprise interpretation and decision-making.

sections.label: Facilitator Guide
sections.sub: Use this tab to prepare before each section. It contains the unit intent, key facilitation questions, and tone and watch points for the full unit.

guidance: ◆ Unit Intent

Before the organisation can define where it is going, leaders must agree on what strategy actually means, in the precise, strategic sense, translated to operational reality, that makes every subsequent decision coherent.
Three connected outputs carry the unit: the Strategy Architecture, the Strategy Intent Statement and Success in Practice. Protect the time in Section 4 for each group to build them in that order.
How the unit runs: Teach the whole unit from the deck first. Participants then go to the portal and complete their own page, in the session or after it.
◆ Key Facilitation Questions
Four questions anchor the unit. Ask each one where it belongs as you teach from the deck.
Sections 1 and 4 · Strategy Architecture: “How well defined is each part of our strategy architecture today?”
1.3, Section 3 and 4.3 · Success in Practice: “If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?”
Section 2 · Decision Filter: “When a new initiative, investment or opportunity appears, what tells us whether it belongs in our strategy?”
Section 5 · Role contribution: “From my executive role, what must I contribute for this Success in Practice to become real?”
◆ Tone & Watch Points
These four points apply when the groups do the work on the portal, after the teaching.
4.2 · Strategy Intent Statement. Watch for: a statement that carries every point from the Architecture. Say: “The Architecture contains the depth. The Intent must provide the clarity.”
4.3 · Success in Practice. Watch for: statements that list initiatives, projects or activities. Bring the group back to observable reality. Ask: “What is happening when the strategy is working?”
4.3 · Balance. Watch for: one perspective defining success for the whole organisation. Use the SiP Flammables as the balance check.
5.1 · Role contribution. Watch for: general statements such as “Support the strategy”. Ask: “What does this role specifically decide, enable, coordinate, resource, protect or change?”

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Interrogative Anchor · What is the Strategy Architecture? What is the Strategy Intent Statement? What is Success in Practice?
slo: Redefine strategy to create a robust understanding of strategy architecture.
Distinguish the direction an organisation sets from the future position that defines its success.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1 · Awareness

Section intent: This section establishes the conceptual bedrock of the entire unit. Before any co-creation can happen, participants must share a single, precise definition of strategy and understand its three building blocks: the Strategy Architecture, the Strategy Intent Statement and Success in Practice. Do not rush this. Every word in the definition has strategic consequence.
◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Opening the Session · Defining Strategy in Your Own Words
Ask: Before showing any content, ask each participant to define strategy in their own words: "Write your definition of strategy in one sentence — right now, without consulting anyone."
Collect: Collect 3–4 responses. Note the differences on a whiteboard. This gap between answers is exactly the problem this unit solves. Use it as the opening provocation.
Keep: Ask every participant to keep their definition. The Unit Summary returns to it.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
Each participant enters their definition of strategy in the box at the top of Section 1 of the participant file: "Opening the Session — Your Definition of Strategy".
Facilitator Script
Set the frame: Before defining strategy, introduce Strategy Architecture as the underlying logic that gives a strategy its structure.

Explain: "Before we can express strategy clearly, we need to understand what sits underneath it. We call this the Strategy Architecture — the interconnected choices and logic that determine what the organisation will do, why, how and when; how it will create, deliver and sustain value; for whom; and within what environment."

Emphasise that the purpose of this section is to unpack the architecture before trying to produce a strategy statement. A strategy can sound compelling while important parts of its underlying logic remain weak, disconnected or undefined.
As participants work through the concepts, ask them to consider: "How well defined is each part of our strategy architecture today?"

Bridge to the definition: "We are now going to unpack the Strategy2Results® definition of strategy. Each concept in the definition represents part of the architecture. Once we understand the parts and how they connect, we can begin constructing a coherent strategic position."

parts.title: 1.1 — Define the Strategy Architecture
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1.1

Taking participants through the 9 concepts: Take the concepts one at a time: what each one means, its strategic implication and what fails when it is missing. Then ask: "Which of these nine concepts is least visible in how your organisation currently talks about strategy?"

Key concept to linger on: The distinction between Thinking & Logic (the cognitive engine) and Process (the structured container). Most organisations have process but neglect thinking quality — the definition forces participants to see this gap.

The Value Triad (Creates · Delivers · Sustains): Draw explicit attention to this concept. Ask: "Is your current strategy as strong on Sustains as it is on Creates and Delivers? Where is the investment in sustainability of value?" This often surfaces an uncomfortable silence.
content: "Strategy is the output of iterative thinking, logic and process to determine what, why, how and when an organisation creates, delivers and sustains value to its stakeholders while navigating the forces within its operating environment."
Every word carries strategic weight. Expand each concept below.

parts.title: 1.2 — Defining the Strategy Intent Statement
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1.2

Positioning the statement: The Strategy Architecture holds the depth and the supporting logic. The Strategy Intent Statement is crisp, directional and easy to express. Participants derive their own statement in Section 4; here they learn what it brings forward.

Taking participants through the 4 dimensions: Walk through WHAT, WHY, HOW, WHEN one at a time as a group. For each, ask one diagnostic question from the content and take 2–3 responses. HOW and WHEN typically reveal the most significant gaps — give them additional time.

HOW — key facilitation moment: Ask: "Does your operating model currently match your strategy — or is it a legacy structure that predates your current direction?" This often opens the most honest conversation of the entire Awareness section.
WHEN: Ask: "Have you actually mapped the sequence of moves needed to achieve your strategy — or does the plan treat all initiatives as running in parallel?"
content: The Strategy Architecture provides the foundation from which the Strategy Intent Statement is derived. It has established the organisation's strategic choices and the logic connecting them.
The Strategy Intent Statement brings forward four dimensions from that architecture. Select each one.
Dimension 1
WHAT
Dimension 2
WHY
Dimension 3
HOW
Dimension 4
WHEN
These four dimensions are then crystallised into one clear Strategy Intent Statement.

The strength of the statement comes from the architecture beneath it. It should therefore be crisp, directional and easy to express, while the Strategy Architecture holds the depth and supporting logic.
The resulting Strategy Intent becomes the organisation's directional anchor for strategic choices, alignment and execution.

parts.title: 1.3 — Success in Practice (SiP): From Intent to Future Reality
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 1.3

The Strategy Intent Statement establishes the ambition. Success in Practice defines what must be seen, experienced and executed for that ambition to become reality within a given time horizon. Defining this together creates a shared picture of success, reducing the risk of different functions interpreting the same strategic intent differently.
Position participants inside the future created by the Strategy Intent. Ask them to imagine that the intent has been successfully realised and describe the observable organisational reality.
The central question: "If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?"

Facilitator emphasis: Keep participants focused on observable reality. The SiP describes what is happening when the strategy is working. Initiatives, projects and activities stay out of it. The aim is shared construction: leaders should leave with a common understanding of what success looks like across the organisation.
content: "If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?"
Success is considered across four observable domains:
D1 · Customer Experience & Value
What customers and other value recipients experience when the strategic intent is working.
D2 · Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm
How the organisation operates, coordinates, delivers and adapts when the capabilities required by the intent are functioning effectively.
D3 · People & Culture Dynamics
How people understand the strategic intent, make decisions, collaborate, take ownership and behave when the intent is embedded in the organisation.
D4 · Enterprise Value Creation
How the organisation benefits across its measures of enterprise success.
Together, the four domains create a shared organisational picture of success against which decisions, trade-offs and execution can be aligned.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: The Importance and Relevance of SiP
sections.sub: Ignition Point · Why do the Strategy Intent and SiP matter once they are defined? How do they shape alignment, choices and execution?
slo: Explain how a shared strategic ambition and a shared picture of success keep leaders and functions aligned.
Recognise how a shared direction filters decisions throughout execution.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2 · Intelligence
Section intent: The Strategy Intent and SiP become useful when they begin to shape how the organisation aligns, makes choices and executes.
Explain that once leaders have established a shared strategic ambition and defined what success looks like in practice, those two outputs become common reference points across the organisation.
They serve three important functions:
Strategic Alignment — keeping people and functions oriented around the same ambition and picture of success.
Decision Filter — providing a basis for determining which choices, opportunities and investments support the strategy.
Execution Coherence — helping different functions understand how their individual contributions must connect to produce the enterprise outcome.

parts.title: 2.1 — Role of Strategy Intent & SiP in the S2R® Architecture
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 2.1

Walk participants through each function and demonstrate how Strategy Intent and SiP work together. The Intent anchors the ambition and strategic choices; SiP anchors the organisational reality those choices are intended to produce.
As you move through the three functions, invite participants to consider: "What happens in an organisation when this function is weak or absent?"
Use the Decision Filter to make the application particularly practical. Ask: "When a new initiative, investment or opportunity appears, what tells us whether it belongs in our strategy?"
The Strategy Intent provides the test of strategic fit. SiP provides the test of strategic contribution: whether the choice moves the organisation closer to the success it has defined.

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.sub: Locate Hot Zones · Depth within each SiP domain · Balance across all four SiP domains
slo: Use observable indicators to examine what success looks like within each of the four SiP domains.
Distinguish between conditions that demonstrate success and signals that those conditions are absent.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3 · Extrapolating

Section intent: We have established that Success in Practice answers a central question: "If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?" This section takes that question deeper.

Each of the four SiP domains covers an important part of organisational reality. Broad statements about customer experience, operational capability, people and culture, or enterprise value fall short. Leaders need to be able to recognise what success would actually look like when it begins to show up in practice.

This is where observable indicators become useful. The indicators help us examine each SiP domain more deeply. They show the kinds of conditions we would expect to observe when that aspect of the Strategy Intent is working, as well as the signals that may indicate something is missing.

There is also a second discipline: balance across the four domains. A leadership team can develop a strong picture of customer success while overlooking the operational capability required to deliver it. It can describe an enabling culture without connecting that culture to enterprise value. It can define strong financial outcomes without describing the customer, operational and people conditions required to produce them.
This section therefore develops two disciplines: Depth within each SiP domain. Balance across all four SiP domains.
We begin by examining the observable indicators within each domain. We then examine what happens when one domain becomes dominant and begins to distort the organisation's overall picture of success.

parts.title: 3.1 — SiP Observable Indicators
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3.1

Each SiP domain is examined through a set of observable indicators. These indicators help leaders move from a broad description of success to the specific conditions through which that success would become visible in the organisation.
For every indicator, examine two positions:
When Working describes what we would expect to observe when that aspect of the SiP is functioning effectively.
Signal of Absence describes what may become visible when that condition is weak, missing or disconnected from the Strategy Intent.
Use both positions to deepen the discussion. Sometimes the absence of a condition provides the clearest evidence of why it matters.
The indicators sit alongside the organisation's SiP. They help leaders test, deepen and make observable the success they have defined.
content: Each SiP domain is examined through a set of observable indicators. Every indicator has two positions: When Working and Signal of Absence.
D1 · Customer Experience & Value
D2 · Operational Capability
D3 · People & Culture
D4 · Enterprise Value

parts.title: 3.2 — SiP Flammables: When the Picture of Success Becomes Distorted
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 3.2
The four SiP domains are designed to describe one organisational reality.

In practice, leadership teams naturally bring different perspectives into the conversation. A commercial leader may see success primarily through customers and growth. An operations leader may emphasise efficiency, process and delivery. A people leader may focus on culture and capability. A finance leader may foreground financial and enterprise outcomes.
Each perspective contributes something important.
The strategic risk emerges when one perspective becomes so dominant that it begins to define success for the entire organisation.
This is what the SiP Flammables are designed to expose.

They provide a balance test for the SiP. They help leaders recognise when a legitimate dimension of success has become disproportionately influential and the enterprise picture has started to narrow into a functional one.
content: The four SiP domains describe one organisational reality. When one perspective becomes dominant, the enterprise picture narrows into a functional one. Expand each pattern to see what it creates, the indicators that reveal it and the strategic risk if it is not balanced.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.h2: Build the Architecture · Derive the Intent · Define Success in Practice
sections.sub: Collective Intelligence of Execution · Strategy Architecture → Strategy Intent → Success in Practice
slo: Build a coherent Strategy Architecture.
Integrate different leadership perspectives into one shared enterprise position.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4 · Integration

Section intent: This is the production section of the unit. Participants now apply the concepts developed through Awareness, Intelligence and Extrapolating to construct the organisation's Strategy Intent Design.

The work happens collectively because strategy requires more than agreement with a finished statement. Leaders need to contribute to the thinking, surface different interpretations, work through tensions and arrive at a position they can collectively own.
Each group will work through three connected stages:
4.1 — Build the Strategy Architecture: Work through the 14 elements, then write the group's Strategy Architecture output.
4.2 — Derive the Strategy Intent Statement: Use the completed architecture to crystallise WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN into one clear statement of strategic ambition.
4.3 — Build Success in Practice: Define what must be seen, experienced and executed across the four SiP domains, confirm each domain statement, and bring the four together into the group's SiP.
Emphasise the sequence. Each output provides the foundation for the next: Strategy Architecture → Strategy Intent → Success in Practice
The quality of the final SiP therefore depends on the quality of the Intent, and the quality of the Intent depends on the thinking captured in the Architecture.

Working in groups: Participants work in their assigned groups throughout the exercise. Encourage groups to surface differences before resolving them. Different interpretations are useful because they expose assumptions, trade-offs and areas where the organisation's strategic thinking is not yet coherent.
The objective is collective construction of one enterprise position.

parts.title: 4.1 — Step 1: Build the Strategy Architecture
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4.1
This is the foundation of the exercise.

Each group works through the 14 elements of the Strategy2Results® Strategy Definition. The purpose is to establish the thinking and logic underneath the organisation's strategic position before attempting to express that position concisely.

Remind participants that the elements are interconnected. A strong answer to one element can expose a weakness or contradiction in another. For example, the value the organisation intends to create must be supported by its HOW; its WHEN must reflect the capabilities that need to be built; and its approach to sustaining value must respond to the forces within its operating environment.
Encourage participants to capture actual strategic choices and to leave broad organisational aspirations out.
As each element is completed, the group should review what it has written and confirm: "Is this what we mean?"
The purpose of confirmation is to ensure that the written position represents the group's thinking before it becomes part of the architecture.

Producing the Strategy Architecture: Once all 14 elements have been completed, the group should step back from the individual responses and examine them as one strategic system. Ask groups to consider: "What is this architecture collectively saying about the organisation's strategy?"

They should then write out their Strategy Architecture output. The output should bring together the major strategic choices and logic revealed through the 14 elements. It should be sufficiently detailed to preserve the thinking underneath the strategy while showing how the different choices connect.
Before finalising, ask groups to check:
Do our choices reinforce one another?
Where are there contradictions or unresolved tensions?
Does our HOW support what we have chosen to achieve?
Does our timing and sequencing reflect the realities of our capability and environment?
Have we addressed how value will be created, delivered and sustained?
Does the architecture represent the strategic position we collectively intend?
The completed Strategy Architecture becomes the source for Step 2.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
The group agrees each entry and one member acts as scribe. Every member then types the agreed entries into their own page of the participant file, in the session or after it.
Each group works in 4.1 of the participant file, one element at a time:
It answers the four questions of the element and selects Generate what this is saying.
The page shows what the group's inputs are saying and asks: "Is this what you mean?"
The group selects Yes, confirm, or No, refine and states what the position should say.
A progress bar counts the confirmed elements. When all 14 are confirmed, the Strategy Architecture output unlocks. The group reviews it, refines it and confirms it. It can then be printed.
The elements, guides and questions below are for your preparation.
content: The 14 elements follow the Strategy2Results® definition of strategy. OUTPUT, the first concept in 1.1, is what the 14 elements produce: the Strategy Architecture. Click each element to expand.
1 · ITERATIVEContinuously refined▼
Guide shown to participants

Strategy is never finished in one pass. It is a hypothesis that loops: form → test against reality → revise → repeat. This rules out strategy as an annual ritual and rules in strategy as a living capability.
The four questions
What core hypotheses does the strategy depend on?
How will reality test those hypotheses?
What evidence would trigger refinement?
How and when will strategic choices be revisited?
2 · THINKING & LOGICThe cognitive engine▼
Guide shown to participants
Thinking = divergent, exploratory, hypothesis-generating. Logic = convergent, analytical, assumption-testing. Both are required in sequence.
The four questions
What alternative possibilities were explored?
What assumptions underpin the preferred direction?
What must be true for this strategy to work?
What evidence supports or challenges the logic?
3 · PROCESSStructured container▼
Guide shown to participants
Process turns ad hoc thinking into a repeatable, auditable, scalable method. It defines who is involved, what inputs are needed, what tools are used, and what decisions get made at each stage.
The four questions
Who must participate in shaping the strategy?
What inputs and evidence are required?
What decision stages will be used?
How will decisions and rationale be recorded?
4 · WHATScope & definition▼
Guide shown to participants
What value are we creating? What business are we actually in? What do we offer and deliberately not offer? This sets the boundary of the organisation's field of play.
The four questions
What business are we actually in?
What value are we choosing to create?
What will we offer?
What will we deliberately not offer or pursue?
5 · WHYPurpose & rationale▼
Guide shown to participants
Why does this organisation exist? Why would stakeholders choose us? The North Star that makes all other decisions coherent and gives the strategy its internal logic.
The four questions
Why does the organisation exist?
Why should stakeholders choose or support us?
Why are these strategic choices appropriate?
What unifying rationale makes the choices coherent?
6 · HOWMechanism & model▼
Guide shown to participants
How do we actually deliver the value? What capabilities, processes, structures and partnerships make it possible? This is where strategy meets the operating model.
The four questions
What operating mechanism makes the strategy work?
Which capabilities are essential?
Which processes and structures must support it?
Which partnerships or ecosystem relationships are required?
7 · WHENTiming & sequencing▼
Guide shown to participants
When do we move? When do we hold? When do we exit? Timing determines whether the right move wins or fails. Sequencing determines whether capability is built in the right order.
The four questions
What must happen first, next and later?
What determines when we move, hold or exit?
Which dependencies shape the sequence?
What timing assumptions could change the strategy?
8 · CREATES VALUEOrigination layer▼
Guide shown to participants
Value comes into existence through creation: product/service development, innovation, capability building, IP, brand equity — activities that generate new or improved worth.
The four questions
What new or improved value will come into existence?
Through which activities is that value created?
What capabilities or assets enable creation?
How will we know that genuine value has been created?
9 · DELIVERS VALUEDistribution & access layer▼
Guide shown to participants
Creating value means nothing if it does not reach intended recipients. Delivery is the full system of transmission: channels, distribution, customer experience, partnerships and pricing.
The four questions
How will created value reach each intended recipient?
Which channels and access mechanisms matter?
What experience must recipients have?
What could prevent value from reaching them?
10 · SUSTAINS VALUEDurability & compounding layer▼
Guide shown to participants
Sustaining requires investment in the conditions that make value possible: relationships, infrastructure, culture, financial health and continued relevance.
The four questions
What makes this value durable over time?
What must be continually invested in or renewed?
What could erode the value?
How will relevance and viability be sustained?
11 · STAKEHOLDERSFull universe of value recipients▼
Guide shown to participants
Broader than customers: everyone with a stake in the organisation's actions, including employees, investors, communities, regulators, partners and future generations.
The four questions
Who has a material stake in our actions?
What value does each stakeholder group receive or contribute?
Where do stakeholder interests reinforce or conflict?
Whose interests could be overlooked by this strategy?
12 · NAVIGATINGActive, skilful movement▼
Guide shown to participants
Navigation implies agency, skill and continuous course correction. Read the environment, interpret it and make deliberate moves through it — putting the forces to use.
The four questions
How will the organisation sense changes in its environment?
How will signals be interpreted and translated into decisions?
Where can external forces be used to advantage?
What enables deliberate course correction?
13 · THE FORCESWhat must be navigated▼
Guide shown to participants
Competitive, macro, disruptive, social and environmental forces shape strategic viability: rivals, substitutes, regulation, economics, technology, business models, ESG and demographic shifts.
The four questions
Which competitive forces materially shape the strategy?
Which macro and regulatory forces matter most?
Which disruptive forces could alter the model?
Which social or environmental forces create risk or opportunity?
14 · OPERATING ENVIRONMENTThe bounded context▼
Guide shown to participants
The full system within which the organisation exists: industry, economy, regulation, technology, social context and physical environment. Strategy only makes sense within a defined environment.
The four questions
What is the defined operating context for this strategy?
Which industry and market conditions shape it?
Which regulatory, technological and social conditions matter?
Where would this strategy stop making sense if the context changed?
The Strategy Architecture Output
The page brings the 14 confirmed elements together under five headings. The group refines the text until it accurately represents the organisation's strategic architecture.
Strategic Position
WHAT · WHY
Strategic Model
HOW · WHEN
Value Architecture
CREATES VALUE · DELIVERS VALUE · SUSTAINS VALUE · STAKEHOLDERS
Strategic Navigation
NAVIGATING · THE FORCES · OPERATING ENVIRONMENT
Strategy Discipline
ITERATIVE · THINKING & LOGIC · PROCESS

parts.title: 4.2 — Step 2: Derive the Strategy Intent Statement
parts.meta: WHAT · WHY · HOW · WHEN → One Strategic Ambition
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4.2
With the Strategy Architecture established, groups now crystallise that thinking into a Strategy Intent Statement.
The Architecture contains the depth. The Intent must provide the clarity.
Bring forward the four dimensions already established through the architecture:
WHAT — the value the organisation has chosen to create and its field of play.
WHY — the rationale for those choices and why they matter.
HOW — the operating model, capabilities and mechanisms through which the value will be delivered.
WHEN — the timing, sequencing and strategic moves through which the ambition will be pursued.
Ask groups to review these four dimensions together and derive one crisp Strategy Intent Statement.

Facilitator emphasis: Protect the Intent from becoming overloaded. Participants may try to carry every important point from the Architecture into the statement. Remind them that the Architecture already holds that detail.
The Strategy Intent Statement crystallises the ambition. The Architecture keeps the detail.
A strong Intent should allow a leader to understand the organisation's strategic position without needing a paragraph of explanation.
Once drafted, have the group read the statement against its completed Architecture and confirm: "Does this statement faithfully express the strategic ambition contained in our Architecture?"
Where the statement exposes a contradiction in the Architecture, resolve the underlying contradiction before finalising the Intent.
The confirmed Strategy Intent becomes the source for Step 3.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY

In 4.2 of the participant file each group sees its own answers for WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN, deduces one crisp Strategy Intent Statement from them and types it in. The group confirms the statement. It can then be printed. Every member types the agreed statement into their own page.
content: The four dimensions brought forward from the architecture:
WHAT
The value the organisation has chosen to create and its field of play.
WHY
The rationale for those choices and why they matter.
HOW
The operating model, capabilities and mechanisms through which the value will be delivered.
WHEN
The timing, sequencing and strategic moves through which the ambition will be pursued.
"Does this statement faithfully express the strategic ambition contained in our Architecture?"

parts.title: 4.3 — Step 3: Build Success in Practice
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 4.3
The Strategy Intent Statement establishes the ambition. The group now defines what must be seen, experienced and executed for that ambition to become reality within the agreed time horizon.
Position the group inside the future described by its Strategy Intent. Use one central question: "If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?"
The group works through the four SiP domains:

1. Customer Experience & Value — Describe what customers and other value recipients experience when the Strategy Intent is working. Use the observable indicators explored in Section 3 to deepen the discussion where useful, but keep the group's final output focused on its specific Strategy Intent. The group produces one Customer Experience & Value statement.

2. Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm — Describe how the organisation operates, coordinates, delivers and adapts when the capabilities required by the Strategy Intent are functioning effectively. The group produces one Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm statement.

3. People & Culture Dynamics — Describe how people understand the Strategy Intent, make decisions, collaborate, take ownership and behave when the intent is embedded in organisational practice. The group produces one People & Culture Dynamics statement.

4. Enterprise Value Creation — Describe how the organisation is benefiting across the measures of enterprise success that matter to this Strategy Intent. The group produces one Enterprise Value Creation statement.

Confirming each SiP domain: After drafting each statement, pause and ask: "Is this what success in this domain should look like if our Strategy Intent is realised?" Refine the statement until the group confirms it.
This is important. The SiP should emerge from the group's own definition of success. Generic descriptions of a successful organisation have no place in it.
Once all four statements are confirmed, place them together and read them as one Success in Practice.
Test the SiP: Use the two quality checks from Section 3.
Depth: Is each statement specific enough that we could recognise the condition if we saw it in practice?
Balance: Do the four statements collectively describe enterprise success, or has one perspective become dominant?
Use the SiP Flammables as the final balance check.
The four confirmed statements together become the organisation's Success in Practice.

Closing Section 4: Each group now holds three connected outputs: its Strategy Architecture, its Strategy Intent Statement and its Success in Practice. Close the exercise by having each group display or print the three together: Strategy Architecture → Strategy Intent → Success in Practice
Then reinforce the connection: The Architecture provides the logic. The Intent crystallises the ambition. Success in Practice makes the ambition observable.
These three outputs become the strategic foundation that subsequent S2R® work will carry into alignment, execution and performance.
📋 PARTICIPANT ACTIVITY
In 4.3 of the participant file, for each SiP domain the group:
answers the three input questions;
derives one statement for the domain from those answers and types it in;
confirms the statement.

The group writes every statement, and every member types the agreed entries into their own page. When all four statements are confirmed, they appear together, numbered 1 to 4, as the group's Success in Practice. The group confirms it. It can then print its three outputs as one report: the Strategy Intent Design.

Into the Capstone: the three confirmed outputs feed the team's Capstone Blueprint. Its Unit 2 section opens once every member of the team has completed Unit 2, and brings the three outputs in from the member's page. The team reads them together and confirms them there.
content: "If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?"
Click each domain to see its lead question and input questions.
D1 · Customer Experience & Value▼
Lead question
If the intent succeeds, what should customers and other value recipients see and experience?
The three input questions
What will customers or value recipients experience differently?
What value or result will they consistently receive?
What observable evidence will tell us this is true?
D2 · Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm▼
Lead question
If the intent succeeds, what should be visible in how the organisation operates and executes?
The three input questions
What capabilities and operating conditions will be functioning effectively?
How will priorities, decisions, coordination and delivery work in practice?
What observable evidence will show that execution is working?
D3 · People & Culture Dynamics▼
Lead question
If the intent succeeds, what should be visible in how people understand, decide and behave?
The three input questions
What will people understand about the strategic intent and their contribution?
How will people decide, collaborate, take ownership and behave?
What observable evidence will show that these conditions are embedded?
D4 · Enterprise Value Creation▼
Lead question
If the intent succeeds, how should the organisation benefit across its success metrics?
The three input questions
What enterprise outcomes should improve as a result of the strategy?
What strategic or market position should the organisation achieve?
What evidence will show that value is being sustained within the time horizon?

sections.label: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
sections.h2: From Success in Practice to Leadership Contribution
sections.sub: Each participant applies the agreed Success in Practice to an executive role and defines what that role must contribute to make the Strategy Intent real.
slo: Apply the agreed Success in Practice to specific executive roles.
Define what each leadership role must contribute to make the Strategy Intent real.

guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5 · Application
Section intent: This section moves the group from the agreed Success in Practice into practical executive contribution.
In Section 4, the group has already produced: Strategy Architecture → Strategy Intent → Success in Practice
Success is already defined. The work in this section is to apply it.
Each participant now asks: "From my executive role, what must I contribute for this Success in Practice to become real?"
The Application section helps the group see whether the agreed strategy is supported by clear leadership contribution, cross-functional ownership and shared accountability.
Sequencing the two activities:
5.1 — Role Contribution to SiP: Each participant completes the table from an assigned executive role
5.2 — SiP Statement Collective Application: Each group shares its SiP statement and explains how the role contributions support it

parts.title: 5.1 — Role Contribution to SiP
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Section 5.1
Purpose: This table captures how each executive role contributes to the agreed Success in Practice.

Ask participants to return to the four SiP statements produced in Section 4: Customer Experience & Value · Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm · People & Culture Dynamics · Enterprise Value Creation.

Each participant now completes the table from the perspective of their assigned executive role. Use this central question: "From this role, what must be contributed so that the agreed Success in Practice becomes real?"
Participants should write in the present tense of the future, as if the strategy is already working. For example:
"Customers experience…"
"Operations are able to…"
"People consistently…"
"The organisation creates value through…"
Encourage practical and role-specific responses. Push back on general statements such as:
"Support the strategy"
"Improve communication"
"Collaborate better"
"Drive performance"
Ask in response: "What does this role specifically decide, enable, coordinate, resource, protect or change?"
After completing the row, each participant should check whether their contribution strengthens all four SiP domains or only reflects the priorities of their own function.
Recording: Each participant enters their own responses in their participant file.

Each participant selects the assigned executive role in 5.1 of the participant file and completes the four domains of the table from that role. The group's four SiP statements from Section 4 are shown above the table.

parts.title: Unit Summary
guidance: ◆ FACILITATOR GUIDANCE — Unit Summary
Closing the unit: Read each of the five summary blocks aloud, or ask participants to read them in turn. The summary is deliberately concise — its role is to crystallise the arc of the unit.

Return to the opening question: Go back to the definitions participants wrote at the start of Awareness. Ask 2–3 participants — "Read your original definition of strategy. What would you change in it now — and why?" The difference between their opening answer and their closing answer is the measure of what Unit 2 produced.
Tangible outputs check: Before closing, confirm with the group that the following have been produced or are in progress:
A Strategy Architecture output from each group
A confirmed Strategy Intent Statement from each group
Four confirmed SiP statements from each group
A role contribution row from each participant

Closing commitment: Ask each participant to complete this sentence privately — "Based on what Unit 2 revealed, the one thing I am committed to doing differently before our next session is…" Invite 2–3 to share. These become the accountability anchors for Unit 3.

Transition to Unit 3: Remind participants — "What we built today is the strategic foundation: the Architecture, the Intent and the Success in Practice. Unit 3 maps that Success in Practice through KISS and defines the OKRs that will measure our progress toward it."

sections.label: Section 1 · Awareness — What
sections.sub: Interrogative Anchor · What is the Strategy Architecture? What is the Strategy Intent Statement? What is Success in Practice?
slo: Redefine strategy to create a robust understanding of strategy architecture.
Distinguish the direction an organisation sets from the future position that defines its success.

content: Opening the Session — Your Definition of Strategy
Write your definition of strategy in one sentence — right now, without consulting anyone.

parts.title: 1.1 — Define the Strategy Architecture
content: Before you can express strategy clearly, you need to understand what sits underneath it. This is the Strategy Architecture: the interconnected choices and logic that determine what your organisation will do, why, how and when; how it will create, deliver and sustain value; for whom; and within what environment.

A strategy can sound compelling while important parts of its underlying logic remain weak, disconnected or undefined. In the S2R® framework, strategy has a specific applied definition. Every word carries strategic weight, and each concept in it is part of the architecture.

"Strategy is the output of iterative thinking, logic and process to determine what, why, how and when an organisation creates, delivers and sustains value to its stakeholders while navigating the forces within its operating environment."
As you work through the concepts, consider how well defined each part of your organisation's strategy architecture is today.
✍✎ Reflection — Strategy Architecture
Which part of your organisation's strategy architecture is least well defined today? What is the consequence?
prompts: ✍✎ Reflection — Strategy Architecture Which part of your organisation's strategy architecture is least well defined today? What is the consequence?

parts.title: 1.2 — Defining the Strategy Intent Statement
content: Your Strategy Architecture is the foundation from which the Strategy Intent Statement is derived. It establishes your organisation's strategic choices and the logic connecting them.
The Strategy Intent Statement brings forward four dimensions from that architecture. Select each one.
Dimension 1
WHAT
Dimension 2
WHY
Dimension 3
HOW
Dimension 4
WHEN
You then crystallise these four dimensions into one clear Strategy Intent Statement.
The strength of the statement comes from the architecture beneath it. Keep it crisp, directional and easy to express. Your Strategy Architecture holds the depth and the supporting logic.
The resulting Strategy Intent becomes your organisation's directional anchor for strategic choices, alignment and execution.
✍✎ Reflection — Strategy Intent
From your assigned executive leader perspective: which dimension (WHAT, WHY, HOW, WHEN) is least clearly defined in your organisation's current strategy? What would clarifying it change?
prompts: ✍✎ Reflection — Strategy Intent From your assigned executive leader perspective: which dimension (WHAT, WHY, HOW, WHEN) is least clearly defined in your organisation's current strategy? What would clarifying it change?

parts.title: 1.3 — Success in Practice (SiP): From Intent to Future Reality
content: Your Strategy Intent Statement establishes the ambition. Success in Practice defines what must be seen, experienced and executed for that ambition to become reality within a given time horizon. Defining this together gives you and your leadership team a shared picture of success, and reduces the risk of different functions interpreting the same strategic intent differently.
Stand inside the future created by your Strategy Intent. Imagine that the intent has been successfully realised and describe the organisational reality you can observe.
"If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?"
Success is considered across four observable domains:
D1 · Customer Experience & Value
What your customers and other value recipients experience when the strategic intent is working.
D2 · Operational Capability & Execution Rhythm
How your organisation operates, coordinates, delivers and adapts when the capabilities required by the intent are functioning effectively.
D3 · People & Culture Dynamics
How people understand the strategic intent, make decisions, collaborate, take ownership and behave when the intent is embedded in your organisation.
D4 · Enterprise Value Creation
How your organisation benefits across its measures of enterprise success.
Together, the four domains give you a shared organisational picture of success against which you align decisions, trade-offs and execution.
Stay with observable reality. Your SiP describes what is happening when the strategy is working. Initiatives, projects and activities stay out of it.

sections.label: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
sections.h2: The Importance and Relevance of SiP
sections.sub: Ignition Point · Why do the Strategy Intent and SiP matter once they are defined? How do they shape alignment, choices and execution?
slo: Explain how a shared strategic ambition and a shared picture of success keep leaders and functions aligned.
Recognise how a shared direction filters decisions throughout execution.

parts.title: 2.1 — Role of Strategy Intent & SiP in the S2R® Architecture
content: Your Strategy Intent and your SiP become useful when they begin to shape how your organisation aligns, makes choices and executes.

Once you and your leadership team have established a shared strategic ambition and defined what success looks like in practice, those two outputs become common reference points across the organisation. They serve three functions within the Strategy2Results® architecture. Click each to expand.
2.1.1 — Strategic Alignment▼
Why It Matters

Strategy fragments when you and other leaders interpret the organisation's ambition differently. Alignment creates a common strategic reference point while allowing each part of the organisation to make the contribution required of it.
Strategy Intent
Creates shared understanding of your organisation's strategic ambition and the choices that define it. You and your fellow leaders are anchored to the same WHAT, WHY, HOW and WHEN.
Success in Practice (SiP)
Creates a shared picture of what successful realisation of that ambition looks like. Functions may contribute differently, but you are all working towards the same organisational reality.
2.1.2 — Decision Filter▼
Why It Matters

Your organisation continuously faces competing opportunities, investments, initiatives and demands. Without a common strategic filter, priorities become shaped by urgency, functional interests or whoever has the strongest influence in the room.
Strategy Intent
Gives you the reference point for determining whether a choice is consistent with your organisation's strategic ambition and the choices already made.
Success in Practice (SiP)
Tests whether that choice contributes to the conditions of success you have defined. It connects each decision to the future reality it is expected to help create.
2.1.3 — Execution Coherence▼
Why It Matters

Strategy is delivered through many functions, teams and decisions acting together. Your function can perform well on its own while the organisation still fails to produce the intended enterprise outcome. Coherence ensures the contributions connect.
Strategy Intent
Gives you the common strategic anchor for interpreting your mandate and your choices in relation to the enterprise ambition.
Success in Practice (SiP)

Shows what the combined contributions must produce across customer value, operational capability, people and culture, and enterprise value. It lets you see beyond your own outputs to the organisational outcome you collectively enable.

How they work together: The Intent anchors the ambition and the strategic choices. SiP anchors the organisational reality those choices are intended to produce. When a new initiative, investment or opportunity appears, the Strategy Intent gives you the test of strategic fit and SiP gives you the test of strategic contribution: whether the choice moves your organisation closer to the success it has defined.
✍✎ Reflection — Three Functions
Which of the three functions is weakest in your organisation today? What happens as a result?
prompts: ✍✎ Reflection — Three Functions Which of the three functions is weakest in your organisation today? What happens as a result?

sections.label: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
sections.sub: Locate Hot Zones · Depth within each SiP domain · Balance across all four SiP domains
slo: Use observable indicators to examine what success looks like within each of the four SiP domains.
Distinguish between conditions that demonstrate success and signals that those conditions are absent.

parts.title: 3.1 — SiP Observable Indicators
content: Each SiP domain is examined through a set of observable indicators. They help you move from a broad description of success to the specific conditions through which that success becomes visible in your organisation.

For every indicator, examine two positions. When Working describes what you expect to observe when that aspect of the SiP is functioning effectively. Signal of Absence describes what may become visible when that condition is weak, missing or disconnected from the Strategy Intent.
Use both positions. Sometimes the absence of a condition gives you the clearest evidence of why it matters.
D1 · Customer Experience & Value
D2 · Operational Capability
D3 · People & Culture
D4 · Enterprise Value
✍✎ Reflection — SiP Indicators
From your assigned executive leader role: which SiP domain shows the most significant gaps in your organisation right now? What is the primary cause?
prompts: ✍✎ Reflection — SiP Indicators From your assigned executive leader role: which SiP domain shows the most significant gaps in your organisation right now? What is the primary cause?

parts.title: 3.2 — SiP Flammables: When the Picture of Success Becomes Distorted
content: The four SiP domains describe one organisational reality. You and your fellow leaders bring different perspectives into the conversation: a commercial leader may see success through customers and growth, an operations leader through efficiency, process and delivery, a people leader through culture and capability, a finance leader through financial and enterprise outcomes.
Each perspective contributes something important. The strategic risk emerges when one perspective becomes so dominant that it begins to define success for the entire organisation.

The SiP Flammables are your balance test. They help you recognise when a legitimate dimension of success has become disproportionately influential and the enterprise picture has narrowed into a functional one. Each pattern below shows what the imbalance creates, the indicators that reveal it and the strategic risk if it is left unbalanced.

sections.label: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
sections.h2: Build the Architecture · Derive the Intent · Define Success in Practice
sections.sub: Work with your group through three connected stages. Each output is the foundation for the next: Strategy Architecture → Strategy Intent → Success in Practice.
slo: Build a coherent Strategy Architecture.
Integrate different leadership perspectives into one shared enterprise position.

parts.title: 4.1 — Step 1: Build the Strategy Architecture
content: This is the production section of the unit, and Step 1 is its foundation. With your group, work through the 14 elements of the Strategy2Results® Strategy Definition. You establish the thinking and logic underneath your organisation's strategic position before you express that position concisely.

The elements are interconnected: a strong answer to one element can expose a weakness or contradiction in another. The value you intend to create must be supported by your HOW. Your WHEN must reflect the capabilities you need to build. Your approach to sustaining value must respond to the forces within your operating environment.

How each element works. Answer the four questions with actual strategic choices and leave broad aspirations out. Select Generate what this is saying. Read the result with your group and ask: "Is this what we mean?" Confirm it, or refine it until it says what your group means. Surface the differences in your group before you resolve them: they expose assumptions and trade-offs.
Working as a group. Your group agrees each entry and one member acts as scribe. Every member then types the agreed entries into their own page, in the session or after it.
Organisation
Strategy period
14-element progress0 of 14 confirmed
Producing the Strategy Architecture
When all 14 elements are confirmed, step back from the individual responses and examine them as one strategic system.
"What is this architecture collectively saying about our organisation's strategy?"

The page brings your 14 elements together under five headings: Strategic Position, Strategic Model, Value Architecture, Strategic Navigation and Strategy Discipline. Before you confirm the output, check:
Do our choices reinforce one another?
Where are there contradictions or unresolved tensions?
Does our HOW support what we have chosen to achieve?
Does our timing and sequencing reflect the realities of our capability and environment?
Have we addressed how value will be created, delivered and sustained?
Does the architecture represent the strategic position we collectively intend?
Your confirmed Strategy Architecture is the source for Step 2.

parts.title: 4.2 — Step 2: Derive the Strategy Intent Statement
parts.meta: WHAT · WHY · HOW · WHEN → One Strategic Ambition
content: With your Strategy Architecture established, your group now crystallises that thinking into a Strategy Intent Statement. The Architecture contains the depth. The Intent must provide the clarity.

Bring forward the four dimensions already established through your architecture. Your group's answers appear under each one. Review the four together, deduce one crisp Strategy Intent Statement and write it in the box.

Protect the Intent from overload. You may want to carry every important point from the Architecture into the statement. The Architecture already holds that detail. The statement crystallises the ambition. A strong Intent lets a leader understand your organisation's strategic position without a paragraph of explanation.
Read your statement against your completed Architecture and confirm:
"Does this statement faithfully express the strategic ambition contained in our Architecture?"
Where the statement exposes a contradiction in your Architecture, resolve the underlying contradiction before you finalise the Intent. Your confirmed Strategy Intent is the source for Step 3.

parts.title: 4.3 — Step 3: Build Success in Practice
content: Your Strategy Intent Statement establishes the ambition. Your group now defines what must be seen, experienced and executed for that ambition to become reality within the agreed time horizon.
Your Strategy Intent Statement
Complete your Strategy Intent Statement in 4.2.
Stand inside the future described by your Strategy Intent and use one central question:
"If our Strategy Intent is successful, what should we see in practice?"

Work through the four SiP domains. In each one, answer the three questions, then derive one statement for that domain from your answers and write it in. Use the observable indicators from Section 3 to deepen the discussion where useful, and keep each statement focused on your own Strategy Intent.

Confirm each domain. After each statement, pause and ask: "Is this what success in this domain should look like if our Strategy Intent is realised?" Refine the statement until your group confirms it. Your SiP comes from your group's own definition of success. Generic descriptions of a successful organisation have no place in it.
Test the SiP
When all four statements are confirmed, they appear together, numbered 1 to 4. Read them as one Success in Practice and test them:
Depth: Is each statement specific enough that you could recognise the condition if you saw it in practice?
Balance: Do the four statements collectively describe enterprise success, or has one perspective become dominant?

Use the SiP Flammables from 3.2 as the final balance check. The four confirmed statements together become your organisation's Success in Practice. Once you have confirmed it, you can print your three outputs as one report: Strategy Architecture → Strategy Intent → Success in Practice.

Into your Capstone. Your three confirmed outputs feed your team's Capstone Blueprint. Its Unit 2 section opens once every member of your team has completed this unit, and brings the three outputs in from your page. Your team then reads them together and confirms them.
